note: Editorial care summaries for Plantivorous. These are general horticultural guidelines, not prescriptions for wild populations. Always use mineral-free water and avoid wild-collected plants.

temperate.label: Temperate bog
temperate.tagline: Cold winters, wet summers and full sun.
temperate.description: The classic hardy carnivore group: North American pitcher plants, Venus flytraps, thread-leaved sundews and hardy butterworts. These plants expect a pronounced winter dormancy, a permanently wet, acidic substrate and as much direct sun as the growing season can provide. In mild climates they can live outdoors all year; in colder or warmer climates the challenge is protecting the roots from hard freezes while still giving the plant a real winter.
temperate.light: Full sun outdoors for at least six hours a day. Indoors, use a powerful full-spectrum LED close to the plant.
temperate.water: Stand the pot in 2–5 cm of rainwater, distilled water or reverse-osmosis water. Keep the mix wet throughout growth. Reduce to just damp during the coldest weeks, but never let the root zone dry completely.
temperate.soil: A 1:1 mix of peat moss and coarse silica sand or perlite. Some growers add a little live sphagnum on the surface. Avoid compost, loam and fertiliser.
temperate.temperature: Warm summers and cool winters. Most species tolerate light frost when dormant, but protect the pots from hard, prolonged freezes.
temperate.dormancy: Essential. Short days and cold temperatures trigger resting buds, dieback or a slow-down. Do not keep temperate plants warm and actively growing through winter.
temperate.feeding: Let them catch their own insects outdoors. Do not add fertiliser to the soil. A very occasional foliar feed at quarter strength is controversial and rarely necessary.
temperate.propagation: Division in late winter or early spring, seed, leaf cuttings for sundews, and rhizome division for pitcher plants.
temperate.problems: Hard water, drying out, warm winter conditions, aphids, botrytis in still air, and squirrels or birds digging in the bog.
tips: Use a large container so the root mass stays cool and evenly wet.
Rainwater is not optional; hard tap water slowly poisons the substrate.
Give pitcher plants a winter check for rot and remove dead growth in early spring.

subtropical.label: Subtropical rosette
subtropical.tagline: Forgiving, frost-sensitive and happy in a bright window.
subtropical.description: Warm-temperate and subtropical rosette sundews, including the Cape sundew and its relatives. They grow quickly, flower freely and tolerate a wide range of conditions as long as the roots stay wet and the light is strong. They do not need a hard winter dormancy, but growth slows in cool, short days.
subtropical.light: Full sun to very bright light. A south-facing windowsill or a strong LED works well. Weak light produces pale, stretched leaves.
subtropical.water: Stand in 1–3 cm of mineral-free water. Keep the tray topped up; these plants dislike drying out.
subtropical.soil: Peat : perlite or peat : silica sand at 1:1. A little live sphagnum on top helps keep humidity high.
subtropical.temperature: Warm to mild: roughly 15–30°C. Protect from frost. Indoors they cope with normal room temperatures.
subtropical.dormancy: No hard dormancy. Growth slows in winter; reduce water slightly but do not let the mix dry out.
subtropical.feeding: Self-catches small insects. Do not fertilise. If grown indoors without insects, a tiny amount of dried bloodworm or a very dilute foliar feed can help, but it is easy to overdo.
subtropical.propagation: Leaf cuttings in water or on wet peat, division, and fresh seed. Many species self-seed.
subtropical.problems: Hard water, mineral build-up, aphids, thrips, and rot when air is stagnant and the mix is too dense.
tips: Repot every one to two years to remove mineral build-up.
A small fan improves airflow indoors and reduces mould.
Remove flower stalks if you want the plant to put energy into leaves.

cape.label: Cape winter-growing
cape.tagline: Wet winters, dry summers and a Mediterranean rhythm.
cape.description: South African winter-rainfall sundews that grow during the cool, wet months and retreat underground or into a resting rosette during the hot, dry summer. The dry summer rest is not optional: keeping these plants wet year-round is the most common reason they fail in cultivation.
cape.light: Full sun during the winter growing season. Keep the rosette compact and colourful.
cape.water: Wet during winter growth. In late spring, stop watering and let the substrate dry out as the plant goes dormant. Resume watering when new growth appears in autumn.
cape.soil: A very open, sandy mix: peat : coarse sand : perlite at 1:2:1. Excellent drainage is essential.
cape.temperature: Cool and mild in winter; hot and dry in summer. Protect from hard frost and from cold, wet summer conditions.
cape.dormancy: Long, dry summer dormancy. Some species die back to a tuber or corm; others form a small resting rosette.
cape.feeding: Self-catches during the growing season. Do not feed during dormancy.
cape.propagation: Seed, division, and tuber or corm separation.
cape.problems: Summer rot, hard water, insufficient light, and premature watering after dormancy.
tips: Mark the pot and keep it completely dry but shaded in summer.
Use deep pots for tuberous and corm-forming species.
Start watering only when you see new growth, not on a fixed calendar date.

pygmy.label: Pygmy sundew
pygmy.tagline: Tiny rosettes, jewel-like colour and gemmae.
pygmy.description: A group of small Australian sundews with compact rosettes and spectacular colour under strong light. They grow through the cool, wet season and survive the dry season as seed or resting buds. Many produce gemmae — tiny leaf-like propagules — in autumn, making them easy to share and propagate.
pygmy.light: Full sun. Strong light keeps the rosettes tight and brings out red, bronze and gold colour.
pygmy.water: Wet during winter growth, then gradually drier in summer. Do not keep the substrate soggy through hot nights.
pygmy.soil: Very sandy peat: peat : coarse sand at 1:3, with a little perlite. Low nutrient content is important.
pygmy.temperature: Cool to mild. Hot, humid nights are more dangerous than dry heat.
pygmy.dormancy: Dry summer dormancy. Many plants die back to a small bud; gemmae may remain dormant in the substrate.
pygmy.feeding: Self-catches tiny insects. Do not feed with anything large enough to damage the rosette.
pygmy.propagation: Gemmae in autumn is the easiest method. Sow them on the surface of wet sandy peat and keep them cool and bright.
pygmy.problems: Damping-off, algae, heat, aphids and disturbance of the shallow roots.
tips: Use shallow pots with a very sandy surface.
Sow gemmae immediately; they lose viability quickly.
Keep the pot cool and airy after gemmae germinate.

tuberous.label: Tuberous sundew
tuberous.tagline: Underground tubers, winter growth and a long dry rest.
tuberous.description: Australian tuberous sundews that disappear underground for the hot, dry summer and emerge with the winter rains. Some form climbing stems; others stay close to the ground. The tuber is the plant's survival organ, and the dry rest is the key to keeping it healthy.
tuberous.light: Full sun during the growing season. Climbing species benefit from a small trellis.
tuberous.water: Wet during winter growth. Stop watering as the leaves yellow in spring. Keep the pot completely dry through summer, then resume watering when the first shoots appear in autumn.
tuberous.soil: Deep, very sandy mix: peat : coarse sand : perlite at 1:2:1. The pot must drain freely.
tuberous.temperature: Cool and mild in winter. Protect from hard frost and from hot, wet conditions.
tuberous.dormancy: Long, completely dry summer dormancy. Tubers can remain dormant for months.
tuberous.feeding: Self-catches during growth. Never feed during dormancy.
tuberous.propagation: Seed, tuber division, and leaf cuttings for some species. Tubers should be handled carefully.
tuberous.problems: Rot from summer watering, shallow pots, hard water, and early watering before shoots appear.
tips: Use pots at least 15–20 cm deep.
Store dormant pots dry and shaded, not cold and damp.
Label the pot: the tuber is invisible for much of the year.

petiolaris.label: Petiolaris complex
petiolaris.description: A challenging group of tropical Australian sundews with hairy leaves and a pronounced wet-season growth spurt. In the wild they experience a hot, humid wet season followed by a dry season, when many die back to a hairy resting bud. Recreating that rhythm is the key to growing them well.
petiolaris.light: Very bright, hot light. Strong light is essential for healthy, compact growth.
petiolaris.water: Wet during the wet season. During the dry-season rest, reduce water and keep the substrate only barely moist.
petiolaris.soil: Sandy peat with excellent drainage: peat : coarse sand : perlite at 1:2:1.
petiolaris.temperature: Hot: roughly 25–35°C during growth. Warm nights and high humidity help.
petiolaris.dormancy: Dry-season dormancy. Plants may lose their leaves and retreat to a hairy resting bud.
petiolaris.feeding: Self-catches. Do not overfeed; the leaves are sensitive.
petiolaris.propagation: Seed, leaf cuttings and division of resting buds.
petiolaris.problems: Cold, wet roots, rot, spider mites in dry air, and failure to break dormancy.
tips: Keep the root zone warm even in winter.
Do not panic when the plant dies back; keep the resting bud barely moist.
Give the plant a real dry-season reduction, not constant wetness.

annual.label: Annual
annual.description: Short-lived carnivores that complete their life cycle in a single season and survive the rest of the year as seed. Annual sundews, rainbow plants and some bladderworts fit here. The trick is to sow fresh seed, keep the seedlings warm and bright, and let the colony self-seed for the next generation.
annual.light: Full sun to very bright light. Seedlings stretch badly in low light.
annual.water: Keep the surface wet while plants are growing. Use a shallow tray and mineral-free water.
annual.soil: Sandy peat: peat : coarse sand at 1:1 or 1:2. The surface should stay open and bright.
annual.dormancy: None. The plant dies after flowering and seeding; the seeds carry the next generation.
annual.feeding: Self-catches tiny insects. Do not fertilise.
annual.propagation: Fresh seed sown on the surface of wet substrate. Many species self-seed if allowed to flower.
annual.problems: Damping-off, algae, seed predation, and losing the colony because the last plants were not allowed to set seed.
tips: Sow small amounts every few weeks for a continuous display.
Let at least one plant self-seed before removing it.
Keep the pot humid but airy; still, warm air invites damping-off.

perennial.label: Woody perennial
perennial.tagline: Deep roots, strong light and a dry-season rest.
perennial.description: Long-lived, woody or rootstock-forming carnivores such as the perennial rainbow plants. They invest in a deep root system and can live for many years, but they resent root disturbance and need a pronounced dry-season rest. Deep pots and patience are the main requirements.
perennial.light: Full sun to very bright light.
perennial.water: Wet during growth; reduce water during the dry-season rest. Do not let the rootstock stay soggy when the plant is dormant.
perennial.soil: Deep, sandy peat with excellent drainage. A mix of peat, coarse sand and perlite works well.
perennial.temperature: Warm to mild. Protect from frost.
perennial.dormancy: Dry-season rest. The plant may die back to a woody rootstock.
perennial.propagation: Seed or careful division of the rootstock. Avoid disturbing established plants.
perennial.problems: Root rot, transplant shock, hard water and insufficient light.
tips: Use the deepest pot you can accommodate.
Do not repot unless the plant is actively growing.
Reduce water, not light, during the resting season.

mediterranean.label: Mediterranean
mediterranean.tagline: Winter growth, summer drought and brilliant light.
mediterranean.description: Species from Mediterranean-climate regions, including the Portuguese dewy pine and the South African Roridula. They grow through the cooler, wetter months and endure a hot, dry summer. Excellent drainage and a dry summer rest are more important than rich soil.
mediterranean.light: Full sun, all day if possible.
mediterranean.water: Water during active growth, then reduce sharply in summer. Cephalotus prefers evenly moist roots; Drosophyllum and Roridula need a drier, very well-drained root zone.
mediterranean.soil: A very open, mineral mix. For Drosophyllum, use coarse sand, perlite and a little peat or leaf mould. For Cephalotus, a sandy peat mix with good drainage.
mediterranean.temperature: Cool to warm, with a pronounced seasonal rhythm. Protect from hard frost.
mediterranean.dormancy: Summer dormancy or slow-down. Keep the plants dry-ish and well ventilated.
mediterranean.feeding: Self-catches. Drosophyllum and Roridula are sensitive to root disturbance and fertiliser.
mediterranean.propagation: Seed for Drosophyllum (sow fresh, dislike transplanting); division or seed for Cephalotus; seed or cuttings for Roridula.
mediterranean.problems: Root rot, summer humidity, transplant shock and hard water.
tips: Sow Drosophyllum in its final pot; it hates being moved.
Use a gritty top dressing to keep the crown dry.
Give Cephalotus cool roots and strong light for the best colour.

mexican.label: Mexican butterwort
mexican.description: Mexican Pinguicula are famous for their two seasonal forms: sticky, carnivorous summer rosettes and tight, succulent winter rosettes. They grow on limestone cliffs and seepages, so they tolerate a slightly alkaline mix and need a dry winter rest. The winter rosette is not dead — it is waiting.
mexican.light: Bright, filtered light to full sun. Indoors, a bright windowsill or LED is ideal.
mexican.water: Wet during summer growth. In winter, let the mix dry almost completely and water only enough to keep the succulent rosette from shrivelling.
mexican.soil: A loose mix of peat, perlite and vermiculite, with a little coarse sand. Some growers add crushed limestone or use a slightly alkaline mix.
mexican.temperature: Warm days and cooler nights. Protect from frost; winter rosettes tolerate cool, dry conditions.
mexican.dormancy: Dry winter dormancy with a small, non-carnivorous rosette. Resume watering when carnivorous leaves appear.
mexican.feeding: Self-catches small insects. Do not fertilise the roots.
mexican.propagation: Leaf cuttings, division, and seed. Winter rosettes can be separated carefully.
mexican.problems: Rot from wet winters, hard water, aphids, and scorching in sudden full sun.
tips: Mark the calendar: the winter rosette needs less water, not more.
Use rainwater; Mexican butterworts are sensitive to minerals.
Leaf cuttings root readily on the surface of damp perlite.

tropical.label: Tropical butterwort
tropical.description: Warm-climate Pinguicula from the Neotropics, including epiphytic and lithophytic species. They lack a hard dormancy and prefer steady warmth, high humidity and a loose, airy root zone. Good airflow is as important as water.
tropical.light: Bright, filtered light. Avoid harsh midday sun through glass.
tropical.water: Keep moist year-round, but never waterlogged. Use mineral-free water.
tropical.soil: Loose, humus-rich epiphytic mix: peat, perlite, orchid bark and a little sphagnum.
tropical.temperature: Warm year-round: roughly 18–28°C. Protect from cold draughts.
tropical.dormancy: None. Growth may slow slightly in cool weather.
tropical.feeding: Self-catches. A very light foliar feed can help in low-insect environments, but avoid overfeeding.
tropical.problems: Rot, fungus gnats, low humidity, and cold, wet roots.
tips: Grow on a humidity tray or in a well-ventilated terrarium.
Keep the crown above the substrate line.
Inspect the rosette centre for mould after cool, damp spells.

lowland.label: Lowland tropical pitcher
lowland.tagline: Warm nights, high humidity and steady heat.
lowland.description: Tropical pitcher plants from low elevations, where nights stay warm and humidity is high. They grow quickly in the right conditions but struggle in cool houses. The main challenge is maintaining warmth at night without sacrificing light and airflow.
lowland.light: Bright, filtered light. Some direct morning sun is fine; protect from scorching midday sun.
lowland.water: Keep the mix evenly moist, never soggy. Use mineral-free water. High humidity is important, but the roots still need air.
lowland.soil: An open epiphytic mix: long-fibre sphagnum, orchid bark, perlite and charcoal. Avoid dense peat.
lowland.temperature: Day 25–32°C; night 20–23°C. Avoid drops below about 18°C.
lowland.dormancy: None. Growth slows slightly in cooler weather.
lowland.feeding: Feed pitchers occasionally with a tiny amount of fish food or dried insects. Do not fertilise the roots.
lowland.propagation: Stem cuttings, basal shoots, and seed. Cuttings root well in live sphagnum.
lowland.problems: Cold nights, root rot, spider mites in dry air, and pitcher loss after repotting.
tips: Use a thermometer at night, not just during the day.
Keep the plant warm but move air around it.
Do not trim healthy pitchers; they are the plant's food source.

highland.label: Highland cloud forest
highland.tagline: Cool nights, bright days and cloud-forest humidity.
highland.description: Pitcher plants from montane and cloud-forest habitats, where days are mild and nights are distinctly cool. The night temperature drop is the defining requirement. Highland species are often slower-growing but long-lived, and many produce spectacular upper pitchers.
highland.light: Bright, filtered light. High-altitude species appreciate strong light with cool roots.
highland.water: Keep the mix moist and very airy. Use mineral-free water and never let the root zone stagnate.
highland.soil: Long-fibre sphagnum, orchid bark, perlite and a little charcoal. Keep it open and acidic.
highland.temperature: Day 18–26°C; night 10–16°C. The night drop is essential, especially for ultra-highland species.
highland.dormancy: None, but growth slows in winter. Do not force growth with heat.
highland.feeding: Feed pitchers sparingly. Highlanders are slow-growing and easy to overfeed.
highland.propagation: Stem cuttings, basal shoots, and seed. Cuttings need cool conditions and high humidity.
highland.problems: Warm nights, root rot, sudden humidity crashes, and stress after shipping.
tips: Measure night temperature; it matters more than day temperature.
Use a cool cellar, greenhouse or terrarium with active night cooling.
Keep the plant in the same spot; highlanders dislike being moved.

intermediate.label: Intermediate tropical pitcher
intermediate.description: The broad middle group of tropical pitcher plants and hybrids that tolerate ordinary warm-temperate conditions. Many popular garden hybrids are intermediate and will grow well in a bright conservatory or terrarium with warm days and mildly cool nights. It is the best starting point for most new Nepenthes growers.
intermediate.light: Bright, filtered light with some direct sun. Protect from hot midday glare.
intermediate.water: Keep the mix moist but airy. Use mineral-free water and allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings.
intermediate.soil: Long-fibre sphagnum, orchid bark, perlite and charcoal in roughly equal parts.
intermediate.temperature: Day 22–30°C; night 16–20°C. A modest night drop is beneficial.
intermediate.dormancy: None. Growth may slow in winter.
intermediate.feeding: Feed pitchers occasionally with small insects or fish food. Do not fertilise the roots.
intermediate.propagation: Stem cuttings, basal shoots, and seed.
intermediate.problems: Root rot, low humidity, spider mites, and pitcher loss after a sudden change in conditions.
tips: Choose a hybrid rather than a fussy species for your first pitcher plant.
Keep the substrate open and the air moving.
Do not panic if the plant drops its pitchers after moving; new ones will follow.

aquatic.label: Aquatic bladderwort
aquatic.tagline: Float, submerge and let the bladders hunt.
aquatic.description: Free-floating or submerged bladderworts and the waterwheel plant. They capture tiny aquatic invertebrates with suction traps and need soft, acidic, mineral-free water. The main enemies are algae, fish, hard water and overheating.
aquatic.light: Full sun to bright light. A shallow outdoor tub is ideal in summer.
aquatic.water: Soft, acidic, mineral-free water. Keep the water clean and moving gently. Avoid hard tap water entirely.
aquatic.soil: No soil. Float the plants, or anchor them lightly to a mesh or a little live sphagnum.
aquatic.temperature: Warm in summer; cool in winter. Some species form turions and die back.
aquatic.dormancy: Cool winter rest or turion formation for temperate species. Tropical species may grow year-round.
aquatic.feeding: They catch their own aquatic microfauna. Do not add fish food or fertiliser to the water.
aquatic.propagation: Division of floating stems, turions, and seed.
aquatic.problems: Algae, duckweed competition, fish and snails, hard water, and summer overheating.
tips: Use a wide, shallow container with a lid of shade cloth to limit algae.
Keep fish out; they eat the plants and the prey.
Harvest a few stems before winter in case the main colony collapses.

terrestrial.label: Terrestrial bladderwort
terrestrial.tagline: Wet soil, tiny bladders and surprising flowers.
terrestrial.description: The easiest bladderworts, growing in wet, sandy peat and catching microscopic soil life with underground bladders. Many spread into a dense carpet and reward growers with orchid-like flowers. They are ideal for a sunny bog tray or a terrarium shelf.
terrestrial.light: Bright light to full sun. Flowering is much better with strong light.
terrestrial.water: Stand in 1–2 cm of mineral-free water. Keep the substrate consistently wet but not stagnant.
terrestrial.soil: Peat : coarse sand : perlite at 1:1:1. A little live sphagnum on the surface helps.
terrestrial.temperature: Warm to mild. Protect from frost unless the species is temperate.
terrestrial.dormancy: Many species slow down or die back in winter; some form small tubers or resting buds.
terrestrial.feeding: Self-catches soil microfauna. Do not fertilise.
terrestrial.propagation: Division, stolon cuttings, and seed. Fragments establish easily.
terrestrial.problems: Algae, moss overgrowth, drying out, and fungus gnats.
tips: Keep the colony slightly crowded; bladderworts seem to grow better that way.
Top-dress with live sphagnum to maintain humidity.
Flower spikes are worth the wait; avoid moving the pot while buds are developing.

epiphytic.label: Epiphytic bladderwort
epiphytic.tagline: Tree-dwelling specialists for the orchid house.
epiphytic.description: Tropical Utricularia from cloud forests and tree trunks, including some of the most spectacular species in the genus. They grow in live sphagnum or on tree-fern fibre and demand high humidity, excellent airflow and cool, stable conditions. These are not beginner plants.
epiphytic.light: Bright, filtered light. Protect from hot direct sun.
epiphytic.water: High humidity; mist regularly and keep the mount or moss moist. Use mineral-free water.
epiphytic.soil: Live sphagnum or tree-fern fibre on a mount, or a very open epiphytic mix in a basket.
epiphytic.temperature: Cool to warm, depending on species; many highland species need a night drop.
epiphytic.dormancy: None, but growth slows in cool or dry periods.
epiphytic.feeding: Self-catches microfauna. Do not fertilise; epiphytes are sensitive to salts.
epiphytic.propagation: Division of stolons, careful cuttings, and seed.
epiphytic.problems: Desiccation, rot in still air, spider mites, and sudden collapse after shipping.
tips: Mount the plant at an angle so water drains away from the crown.
Use a fan; high humidity without airflow is a rot trap.
Keep a backup division in a different spot.
